title: How Gene Patents Work
summary: Josh and Chuck explain gene patents: the history of patent rulings on natural products and living things (Telegraph electromagnetism, adrenaline, bacteria cases, the Plant Patent Act of 1930, Diamond v. Chakrabarty), the 1980s human growth hormone and insulin patents, the late-1990s genome-mapping rush and the 2001 USPTO guidelines, patent criteria (useful, non-obvious, novel, enablement), the four categories of gene patents (diagnostics, functional, process, composition of matter), the Myriad Genetics BRCA1/BRCA2 controversy, ethical and economic arguments for and against, and Monsanto's terminator seed technology. The episode opens with banter about the hosts' travel and a Facebook contest, and closes with a listener mail segment about Turkey and a sign-off.

entities.name: United States Patent and Trademark Office

segments.title: Opening banter
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck chat about their weekend travel plans, a friends' wedding in New York, and a Facebook contest that helped the friends win a wedding prize.

segments.title: Growth hormone history and cadaver extraction
segments.summary: The hosts introduce growth hormone deficiency, explaining that growth hormone was once extracted from cadaver pituitary glands at high cost, until Novo Nordisk's recombinant product, nano one, was patented in 1982 after being created in 1973.

segments.title: Early US patent rulings on natural things
segments.summary: A history of court rulings: Robert Morse's telegraph patent was initially denied because it involved electromagnetism, a principle of nature; a 1912 ruling allowed patenting a distilled adrenaline; a post-World War Two Supreme Court ruling denied a patent on a bacteria mixture not found in nature.

segments.title: Plant Patent Act and Luther Burbank
segments.summary: The Plant Patent Act of 1930 allowed patents on plants, credited to botanist Luther Burbank, who created more than 800 strains and varieties; bacteria remained excluded under traditional rulings. A 1970 Plant Protection Act also allowed plant patents.

segments.title: Diamond v. Chakrabarty and composition of matter
segments.summary: Ananda Chakrabarty, who worked for GE, developed a bacterium that breaks down crude oil. After appeals, the Supreme Court in 1980 ruled under the phrase composition of matter that the living bacterium could be patented, a decision that changed patent law.

segments.title: First gene patents and the genome rush
segments.summary: The first gene patent was issued to the University of California within two years, followed by insulin in the same year. In the late 1990s, as the human genome was nearly mapped, a flood of patent applications arrived; in 2001 the USPTO issued guidelines requiring applicants to know what a gene does or to have a process using it.

segments.title: Patent criteria and the first-to-invent rule
segments.summary: The hosts explain patent criteria: useful, non-obvious, novel, and enablement. They describe the twenty-year exclusivity granted in exchange for disclosure, the first-to-invent principle, and the Budapest Treaty culture depositories where biological samples must be filed. They also mention Elisha Gray and Alexander Graham Bell as a telephone priority dispute.

segments.title: Four categories of gene patents
segments.summary: Gene patents break down into four categories: diagnostics (testing for mutations and markers), functional (roles genes play, leading to genetically tailored drugs), process (methods of extracting or manipulating genes), and composition of matter (products like insulin and human growth hormone). Diagnostics and composition of matter are the most controversial.

segments.title: Myriad Genetics BRCA patents and ethical debate
segments.summary: Myriad Genetics patented BRCA1 and BRCA2 breast and ovarian cancer screening, then sent letters to cancer labs demanding payment. Canada and Europe largely ignored the patents, while US courts went back and forth, with the Federal Circuit reversing a 2010 district court decision in 2011. The hosts then discuss the ethical and economic arguments: incentives for research versus monopoly pricing and access, with the AMA opposing the patents.

segments.title: Monsanto terminator seed technology
segments.summary: Monsanto's genetic use restriction technology, known as terminator technology, makes seeds sterile so farmers must buy new seed each year. The hosts note Monsanto vowed not to release it commercially but its contracts restrict seed reuse, and it acquired Delta and Pine Land Company.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts recommend further reading and the documentary The Corporation, and give contact information.
